overview.title: Getting the mini-C4 data, compute expectations, and choosing SentencePiece
overview.main_topic: Downloading and inspecting the mini-C4 pretraining shards, the compute cost of running chapter 16, and the decision to tokenize with SentencePiece and a premade 32,000-term vocabulary.
overview.central_idea: Pretraining starts with a lot of raw text (50 shards of about 75 MB, one web document per line) and a fast subword tokenizer to turn it into integers. This is the most compute-intensive chapter of the book.
overview.importance: Everything the mini-GPT learns comes from this data and this tokenization, and the sidebar sets practical expectations (about 6 hours on a free T4, a little over an hour on an A100) before you start.

Describe the mini-C4 layout: 50 shards, about 75 MB each, one document per line with escaped newlines.
Plan compute for the chapter: T4 vs A100 timings, restarting the runtime to free memory, cutting training steps for experiments.
Explain why a fast tokenizer matters for LLM pretraining and how SentencePiece relates to the BPE tokenizer built in chapter 14.
State the vocabulary size used for the mini-GPT (32,000).

summary:
**Listing 16.1 (continued).** `keras.utils.get_file(fname="mini-c4", origin="https://hf.co/datasets/mattdangerw/mini-c4/resolve/main/mini-c4.zip", extract=True)` downloads a zip of the C4 subset from Hugging Face, caches it and extracts it. The code then builds `extract_dir = pathlib.Path(extract_dir) / "mini-c4"`, the folder that holds the shard files.

**Sidebar: Running the code in this chapter.** Generative LMs are big, and this is the **most compute-intensive chapter in the book**. On the free **Colab T4** GPU the mini-GPT takes **about 6 hours** to train, and you must **restart the runtime** partway through to free GPU memory before loading a larger pretrained model. On an **A100** the whole chapter runs in **a little over an hour**. You can read the expensive `fit()` calls and **reduce the number of training steps** for quick experiments. Future hardware may make all of this trivial.

**The data.** There are **50 shards**, each with **about 75 MB** of raw text, about 3.75 GB in total. **Each line is one crawled document**, with its newlines escaped as the two characters `\n`. Printing the first 100 characters of the first line of `shard0.txt` (after turning the escapes back into real newlines) shows a web page: *"Beginners BBQ Class Taking Place in Missoula! Do you want to get better at making delicious BBQ? You"*.

**Tokenization.** Even a mini LLM needs a lot of preprocessing, so a **fast tokenizer** helps. The chapter uses **SentencePiece**, a C++ library for **subword tokenization**. The authors say its technique is the same byte-pair encoding built by hand in chapter 14, but it is faster and adds a `detokenize()` function that maps integers back to strings and joins them. A **premade 32,000-term vocabulary**, stored in SentencePiece's own format, is used. Listing 16.2 on p.496 loads it.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The dataset has 50 shards of about 75 MB of raw text each. Each line holds one crawled document with its newlines escaped. The code prints the start of the first document in the first shard.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Escaping newlines lets 'one line = one document', so a line-based reader such as tf.data.TextLineDataset (p.496) returns whole documents. The escapes must then be turned back into real newlines, which the snippet does with .replace("\\n", "\n").
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This file format drives the preprocessing pipeline in Listing 16.3. Splitting the data into shards lets it be read in parallel with interleave.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: 50 x 75 MB is about 3.75 GB of text. At roughly 4 characters per token that is about 1 billion tokens, consistent with p.497's 'just under a billion tokens'.

paragraphs.what_it_says: LLM pretraining, even for a mini model, needs a lot of preprocessing, so a fast tokenization routine for turning documents into integer tokens makes life easier.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Tokenization runs on the CPU. If it is slow, the GPU waits. With about a billion tokens, a pure-Python tokenizer would become the bottleneck.

paragraphs.excerpt: We will use SentencePiece, a library for subword tokenization of text data.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The chapter uses SentencePiece for subword tokenization. The authors say the technique is the same byte-pair encoding built in chapter 14, but the library is written in C++ for speed and adds detokenize() to turn integers back into joined strings. A premade 32,000-term vocabulary in SentencePiece format is used.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The algorithm is familiar, and only the implementation and vocabulary file are new. A 32,000-token vocabulary sets the size of the model's input embedding and output softmax.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The vocabulary size becomes vocabulary_size in the model (p.497). The detokenize() function is needed to read generated text.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: SentencePiece works on raw text including spaces (encoded as the '▁' symbol), so detokenization is lossless. It supports both BPE and unigram-LM models. The book says this vocabulary uses BPE.

terminology.meaning: A C++ library (with Python bindings) for subword tokenization that treats text as a raw character stream.
A subword method that starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token.
The inverse of tokenization: map ids back to text pieces and join them.

concepts.name: Pretraining corpus
concepts.definition: The large unlabeled text collection used for next-token pretraining.
concepts.technical: Here: mini-C4, 50 shards of about 75 MB, one document per line with escaped newlines.
concepts.significance: Its size (about 1B tokens) and content (web text) determine what the mini-GPT can learn.
concepts.example: 'Beginners BBQ Class Taking Place in Missoula!'
concepts.misconception: That web text is clean prose. Even 'Clean' Crawled Corpus documents include ads and boilerplate, as the BBQ class example shows.

concepts.name: Subword tokenization
concepts.definition: Splitting text into pieces between characters and words, each mapped to an integer id.
concepts.intuition: Common words become one token. Rare words are spelled with several pieces.
concepts.technical: BPE learns merge rules. SentencePiece applies a premade vocabulary of 32,000 pieces quickly in C++.
concepts.significance: It sets the model's vocabulary_size and how many tokens a text costs.
concepts.misconception: That tokens are words. A word can be split into several tokens, and punctuation gets its own.

concepts.name: SentencePiece
concepts.definition: A fast C++ subword tokenization library with tokenize and detokenize operations.
concepts.intuition: A compiled, production-grade version of the BPE tokenizer from chapter 14.
concepts.technical: It treats whitespace as part of tokens, so detokenization is exact. It is wrapped as a Keras layer by KerasHub (p.496).
concepts.significance: Tokenizing about 1B tokens on CPU needs a fast implementation.
concepts.misconception: That SentencePiece is a different algorithm from BPE. Per the book, the technique here is the same BPE, only faster.

extract_dir = keras.utils.get_file(
    fname="mini-c4",
    origin=(
        "https://hf.co/datasets/mattdangerw/mini-c4/resolve/main/mini-c4.zip"
    ),
    extract=True,
)
extract_dir = pathlib.Path(extract_dir) / "mini-c4"
code.what_it_does: Downloads the mini-c4 zip from Hugging Face, caches and extracts it, and builds the path to the folder that holds the shard files. The listing's caption and imports (import keras, import pathlib) are on p.494.

pathlib's / operator appends the subfolder 'mini-c4', where shard0.txt ... shard49.txt live.

Output: the start of a crawled web page about a BBQ class, now split over two lines because its newline was restored.

pitfalls: In Python source "\\n" is the two characters backslash and n, while "\n" is a newline. Mixing them up leaves escapes in the text or does nothing.

deeper.title: Sanity-checking the data size against the token count
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, using the book's numbers:

- Raw text: $50 \times 75\,\text{MB} \approx 3.75\,\text{GB}$.
- p.497 reports 29,373 batches of $128 \times 256$ tokens, so $29{,}373 \times 32{,}768 \approx 9.6\times10^{8}$ tokens.
- Bytes per token: $3.75\times10^9 / 9.6\times10^8 \approx 3.9$, which is typical for English subword tokenizers with about a 32k vocabulary (roughly 4 characters per token).

So the numbers are consistent.

deeper.title: Why restart the runtime?
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): deep learning frameworks usually keep GPU memory in a pool after a model is no longer used, and Python may still hold references to the model, optimizer state and cached datasets. On a 16 GB T4, the trained mini-GPT plus its optimizer state leaves too little room for a multi-billion-parameter pretrained model. Restarting the process is the most reliable way to release everything.

takeaways: Listing 16.1 downloads and extracts mini-C4 with keras.utils.get_file and points extract_dir at the shard folder.
This is the book's most compute-intensive chapter: about 6 h on a free T4, a little over 1 h on an A100. Restart the runtime before loading the big pretrained model.
The data is 50 shards of about 75 MB, one web document per line with newlines escaped.
Fast tokenization matters at this scale. SentencePiece (C++, BPE per the book) with a premade 32,000-term vocabulary is used.

questions.question: How is a single document stored in the mini-C4 shard files?
options: As one line per document with newlines escaped
As a JSON object per document
questions.answer: As one line per document with newlines escaped
questions.explanation: The page says 'Each line contains a document in the crawl with newlines escaped.' The files are raw text, not JSON or token ids, and there are 50 shards rather than one file per document.

questions.question: Why does the code call .replace("\\n", "\n") when printing a document?
questions.answer: To turn the escaped two-character sequence backslash-n back into real newline characters, so the document's original line structure is restored.
questions.explanation: Newlines were escaped so that each document fits on one line. Unescaping recovers the text, and Listing 16.3 does the same with tf.strings.regex_replace (p.496).

questions.question: How much raw text does the mini-C4 subset contain in total, and roughly how many tokens is that at about 4 characters per token?
questions.answer: 50 x 75 MB = 3.75 GB, which is roughly 0.9-1 billion tokens.
questions.explanation: $3.75\times10^9 / 4 \approx 9.4\times10^8$, consistent with p.497's 'just under a billion tokens'.

questions.question: According to the page, what does SentencePiece offer compared with the tokenizer built in chapter 14?
options: A different algorithm that does not use merges
The same BPE technique, implemented in C++ for speed, plus a detokenize() function
Word-level tokenization with no unknown tokens
questions.answer: The same BPE technique, implemented in C++ for speed, plus a detokenize() function
questions.explanation: The page says the 'actual tokenization technique is the same as the byte-pair encoding tokenization we built ourselves' and that the library is in C++ and adds detokenize(). It is not a word- or character-level tokenizer.

questions.question: What vocabulary size is used for the mini-GPT's tokenizer?
questions.explanation: Stated in the final paragraph. It will become the model's vocabulary_size.

questions.question: Why does the sidebar tell you to restart the Colab runtime partway through the notebook?
questions.answer: To free GPU memory held by the mini-GPT work before loading a larger pretrained model. On a T4 there would not be enough memory for both.
questions.explanation: The sidebar says you 'will need to restart your Colab runtime in the middle of the notebook to free up GPU memory before loading a larger pretrained model.'

questions.question: Before running the chapter, can you decide what hardware you will use, how long training will take, and how you would shorten it for a quick test?
questions.answer: For example: on a T4, expect about 6 hours for the mini-GPT, or cut the training steps in the fit() calls. On an A100, expect a little over an hour end-to-end.
questions.explanation: These are the planning points from the sidebar.
